Abstract
Digital rock physics has increasingly become an emerging field in which advanced numeri-
cal simulation and high-resolution imaging are combined to accurately predict rock prop-
erties. In this context, multiscale imaging is crucial for fully capturing the inherent het-
erogeneity of natural rocks. However, limitations in resolution and field of view (FOV) 
present significant challenges. Direct numerical simulations at large scales are often not 
computationally practical or may be too expensive. The compromise between FOV and 
resolution is particularly pronounced in the complex multiscale pore structures of porous 
rocks, including carbonates in particular. To address this issue, we propose an innovative 
machine learning technique that integrates multiscale imaging data at varying resolutions. 
For the rock sample, we used the imaging data published by Nabipour et al. (Adv Water 
Resour 104695, 2024) in three resolutions. Our approach employs an optimized neural net-
work design combined with a transfer learning strategy, enabling the identification of com-
plex cross-scale correlations that were previously unattainable with conventional methods. 
The results demonstrate that this multiscale neural network approach effectively estimates 
permeability by analyzing various aspects of pore morphology across different scales. In 
particular, we achieved high accuracy, as evidenced by R-squared coefficients of 0.966 for 
training and 0.836 for testing in low-resolution domains, and also significantly enhanced 
computational efficiency, reducing the overall computational time. Despite being tested for 
images of carbonate rocks, the developed method is adaptable to a wide range of multiscale 
porous materials and offers a promising solution to the persistent challenge of balancing 
imaging resolution with FOV.

1  Introduction
Digital Rock Physics (DRP) is a rapidly advancing field that integrates advanced computa-
tional methods with state-of-the-art imaging technologies. It allows for numerical simula-
tions on high-resolution 3D rock images to evaluate various rock properties, such as per-
meability (Sadeghnejad et al. 2021). Offering a non-destructive alternative to traditional 
experimental core analysis, DRP facilitates more precise evaluations of fluid flow and 
solute transport in porous materials. The simulation tools in DRP can mimic processes 
involved in subsurface engineering activities, such as single- and multi-phase flow, par-
ticle transport, and chemical interactions like precipitation, dissolution, adsorption, and 
desorption (Fu et al. 2023). However, as the size of digital rock samples increases, so do 
the computational time and memory requirements of direct numerical simulation (DNS)-
based algorithms (Santos et al. 2020). Standard 3D digital rock images can now reach sizes 
of typically 20,003 voxels, but this scaling introduces practical limitations due to signifi-
cant computational expenses. Consequently, balancing image resolution and field of view 
(FOV) remains a central challenge in DRP, especially in their practical applications (Yan 
et al. 2023; Suhrer et al. 2020). High-resolution micro-CT images provide detailed insights 
suitable for direct simulation techniques like Lattice Boltzmann but struggle with larger-
scale heterogeneities essential for understanding complex porous materials. In contrast, 
lower-resolution images cover a broader FOV but lack the precision for direct permeability 
simulation in larger-scale systems (Botha and Sheppard 2016).
This compromise is particularly critical in complex rocks such as carbonates, which are 
known for their heterogeneity, anisotropy, and multiscale nature. These rocks possess a 
varied pore structure, including interparticle pores, sub-resolution nanometer pores, vugs, 
and microfractures, often not fully capturable in a single micro-CT image (Mehmani et al. 
2020; Sun et al. 2019). Therefore, a method bridging high-resolution and low-resolution 
imaging is vital for accurately predicting transport properties in tight carbonate rocks. Mul-
tiscale imaging and modeling present a promising approach to address this issue, espe-
cially when applied to carbonates. This technique uses low-resolution images to capture 
larger rock features and high-resolution images for detailed characterization of smaller rock 
subvolumes. By integrating data across scales, researchers aim to create a comprehensive 
rock characteristic profile. The challenge lies in effectively combining multiscale data and 
ensuring the representativeness of chosen subvolumes for the entire sample. Additionally, 
the computational linking of images presents a significant challenge that remains unre-
solved (Jackson et al. 2021; Yan et al. 2023).
With advancements in machine learning, researchers are now applying these algorithms 
to various mathematical and engineering challenges (Pal et al. 2023). In DRP, machine 
learning algorithms have been increasingly used for accelerating numerical modeling and 
property estimation (Tembely et al. 2021; Tian et al. 2021; Sudakov et al. 2019; Srisutthi-
yakorn 2016; Röding et al. 2020; Tembely and AlSumaiti 2019; Fu et al. 2023), including 
addressing the balance between image resolution and FOV (Liu et al. 2023; Pal et al. 2023). 
Multiscale 3D micro-CT scan images representing rock samples at various scales facilitate 
the training of machine learning models to recognize and integrate scale correlations. In a 
notable study, Dehghan Khalili (2013) applied renormalization to estimate permeability in 
carbonate rocks using porosity–permeability relationships derived from micro-CT images. 
Similarly, Botha and Sheppard (2016) employed a multiscale statistical method for perme-
ability prediction in sandstone samples, using low-resolution images and high-resolution 
derived permeability computations. However, given the nonlinear relationship between

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become a mainstay in pore-scale modeling 
and flow transport prediction, largely due to their success in computer vision. By using 
convolution layers to automatically extract spatial features from image data, CNNs elimi-
nate the need for manual feature selection and excel at handling complex image inputs (Fu 
et al. 2023). Consequently, many studies have developed CNN-based surrogate models that 
integrate multiscale digital rock analysis. These models aim to balance the field-of-view 
and resolution tradeoff while predicting permeability and other transport properties from 
2D or 3D microstructures at single or multiple scales. (Jiang et al. 2022; Kamrava et al. 
2021, 2020; Liu et al. 2023; Najafi et al. 2021; Rabbani et al. 2020; Santos et al. 2023, 
2021; Tang et al. 2022; Nabipour et al. 2024). Despite the growing body of work on CNN-
based digital rock analysis, current approaches still face key limitations. First, training data 
are often scarce: robust CNNs require large numbers of high-quality images, and acquiring 
3D digital rock data—especially at multiple resolutions—can be prohibitively expensive. 
As a result, many studies resort to 2D or small 3D images or rely on sphere packing for 
microstructure–transport relationships. Second, 3D CNNs demand substantial memory and 
computational resources, typically requiring high-performance computing (HPC) to pro-
cess large representative elementary volumes (REVs) (Fu et al. 2023). Furthermore, most 
existing models assume a single-scale or single-resolution pore structure, which often fails 
to capture the multiscale textures characteristic of carbonates, sandstones, volcanic rocks, 
shales, or coal beds. In some cases, researchers rescale multi-resolution inputs to a uniform 
voxel size, a practice that can obscure critical textural differences (Elmorsy et al. 2022; Liu 
et al. 2023).
To address these limitations, we propose a computationally efficient multiscale machine 
learning model that combines multi-resolution micro-CT images of tight carbonates with 
diverse pore structures. The model accurately estimates effective permeability for lower-
resolution scans covering larger fields of view while leveraging fine-scale insights from 
high-resolution images. In doing so, it bridges the gap between direct pore-scale simula-
tions and larger-scale representative volumes. We implement a multi-layer perceptron 
(MLP) known for its universal approximation properties and lower computational demand 
compared to 3D CNNs, ensuring a balance between accuracy and resource efficiency (Al-
Zubaidi et al. 2023). We train the MLP regression model on robust morphological flow 
descriptors and permeability data derived from high-fidelity LBM simulations on high-res-
olution subvolumes. We explore transfer learning to further enhance accuracy and general-
izability—especially for lower-resolution images where direct simulation is infeasible. This 
strategy adapts the model to new samples with different pore structures and resolutions, 
extending its predictive power beyond the original training set.
This paper aims to present a computationally efficient methodology for predicting and 
mapping variations in permeability within multiscale porous media, with a particular 
focus on carbonate rocks. We used the imaging data published by Nabipour et al. (2024) 
for a highly microporous carbonate in three resolutions. The approach uses a data-driven 
method to investigate the relationship between microstructural characteristics and mac-
roscopic flow transport properties. Although the primary focus is on the permeability of

2  Methodology
The primary goal of this study is to integrate recent advancements in Digital Rock Physics 
(DRP) and artificial intelligence by utilizing a neural network framework complemented 
by a transfer learning strategy. We aim to develop a systematic approach for predicting and 
mapping variations in effective permeability using low-resolution micro-CT images, which 
offer a wider field of view. Additionally, the study includes a comparative analysis with a 
Support Vector Regression (SVR) model to further evaluate our proposed methodology. 
Although lower-resolution binary segmented images may not fully capture the complete 
pore structure, they are hypothesized to contain critical information about important fluid 
flow channels.
This section outlines the implementation of the neural network, following the prepara-
tion and description of the carbonate sample images via DRP. Figure 1 provides a visual 
summary of the workflow, which is detailed in the subsequent points:
1.	 Micro-CT 3D imaging of the carbonate core plug at three spatial resolutions: Low-
resolution (LR), Middle resolution (MR), and High resolution (HR).
2.	 Preliminary preparation and processing of the images.
3.	 3D digital image registration of the images at the three resolutions to identify the over-
lapping region.
4.	 Calculation of transport properties, such as effective porosity and permeability, using 
digitally representative elementary volumes (REV).
5.	 Extraction of representative morphological and topological pore features to create the 
dataset.
6.	 Development and calibration of a multiscale machine learning (ML) model in the reg-
istered overlapping region containing all three image resolutions.
7.	 Evaluation of the model’s performance using test data, estimation of the effective perme-
ability of the LR volumes utilizing the larger FOV of the non-overlapping region, and 
scaling up the results to the scale of the largest LR micro-CT image.
8.	 Construction of an additional ML model (SVR) for further assessment and comparison.

2.1.2  Image Processing
Successful digital rock modeling heavily depends on robust image processing and prepara-
tion. We previously detailed how we registered the sample’s images across multiple reso-
lutions, ensuring consistent alignment for the subsequent analysis (Nabipour et al. 2024). 
In this paper, a brief description of the image processing protocol is given as follows: (1) 
Removing edge artifacts observed in the initial and final top-view slices of each image 
resolution by cropping the images to focus on the interior slices of the core images. (2) 
Enhancing gray intensity or performing histogram equalization to improve contrast and 
adjust the histograms of the images—a necessary step despite its potential to affect some 
structural input image data (Schlüter et al. 2014). (3) Applying a non-local means filter 
with a one-pixel local neighborhood for denoising and smoothing the images, employing 
a technique that uses weighted means determined by blocks instead of individual pixel 
proximity, which effectively reduces noise while preserving contrast boundaries (Sun et al. 
2017). (4) Conducting 3D to 3D image registration to determine the volume of overlap 
between the images and integrate features from all three resolutions, a process that involves 
fusing volumes with varying voxel sizes and enhancing the "similarity" of the 3D images 
by considering their translation, rotation, and scaling properties (Sok et al. 2010). Figure 3 
illustrates the registered images, showing the HR domain (with the smallest field of view), 
the MR tomogram, and the LR tomogram (with the widest field of view) of the carbonate 
plug, as well as the overlapping region of the three resolution images. (5) Segmentation of 
the images is crucial as it dictates subsequent analysis and outcomes, where grayscale data 
is categorized into pore and solid phases. Initially executed using the Otsu method (Andrä 
et al. 2013; Saxena et al. 2017b), the segmentation was then refined following a thorough 
inspection of the pore space (Miarelli and Della Torre 2021), ensuring the resulting poros-
ity was verified against laboratory data.

additional data conversions (Fu et al. 2023). The bounce-back condition in LBM simplifies 
boundary condition handling, and complex geometries can be efficiently represented using

2.2.1  REV Analysis
Creating a REV is pivotal in linking pore-scale insights to continuum-scale transport prop-
erties in porous media. A key step in the DRP workflow involves determining the smallest 
field of view that accurately represents the entire rock sample for a specific attribute (Sax-
ena et al. 2017a). The REV signifies the scale at which the calculated property becomes 
scale-independent or represents the minimum volume where microscopic variations in the 
observed properties of a porous medium are negligible. Reliable REV estimation stream-
lines imaging and computation, preventing the misinterpretation of local inaccuracies as 
macro-scale effects. Determining an appropriate REV is, therefore, vital for upscaling 
petrophysical properties across multiple length scales (Mostaghimi et al. 2013; Singh et al. 
2020).
In this study, we aimed to assess the variations in calculated permeability by the Lattice 
Boltzmann Method (LBM) for high-resolution (HR) carbonate images concerning sample 
size. We selected dimensions where permeability changes remained below 20% (Saxena 
et al. 2017a). Consequently, we identified representative elementary volumes (REVs) for 
the core image using 3D subvolumes of 3003 voxels. We analyzed only connected pore 
space since isolated pores do not contribute to permeability. Using a 26-neighborhood sys-
tem, any voxel sharing at least one vertex was classified as connected. LBM computations 
were performed on a CPU-based system equipped with 64 GB of RAM and four 2.3 GHz 
Intel Xeon processors.
2.3  Dataset Construction
After establishing permeability variations as target labels using high-resolution REVs in 
the previous phase, this crucial stage involves selecting representative features that capture 
the morphological and topological characteristics of the pore space. Unlike some previ-
ous studies that used averaged morphological features from segmented images as machine 
learning model predictors (Botha and Sheppard 2016; Dehghan Khalili 2013; Menke et al. 
2021; Fu et al. 2023), this study employs the three-dimensional Euclidean distance trans-
form (EDT) of the pore phase at each resolution/scale. The EDT assigns a distance value to 
each voxel based on its proximity to the nearest solid boundary, effectively representing the 
radius of the largest sphere that fits within each voxel in the pore space (Santos et al. 2020). 
This feature is sensitive to the cylindrical profile of laminar flow and correlates nonlin-
early with transport parameters in complex porous media (Santos et al. 2020, 2021, 2023). 
Although low-resolution images do not fully capture every pore detail, they still preserve 
key flow pathways that align with the more detailed MR and HR images.
Advantages of training the machine learning (ML) model with EDT include: 
(1)	 Enhanced representation of pore space: EDT maps provide a more comprehensive 
depiction of the pore space morphology and geometry compared to binary segmented 
images. They include details about pore size, configurations, and connectivity, which 
are closely linked to transport properties such as permeability. Training the model with

2.4  Machine Learning Model Development
Extensive research has focused on predicting permeability using neural network-based 
regression algorithms with high-resolution images of porous media. However, there 
has been comparatively less exploration in estimating transport properties using the 
morphological characteristics of realistic and multiscale porous media. In supervised 
machine learning, regression models are utilized to predict continuous values, and 
a wide spectrum of such models is available. The selection of an appropriate model 
largely depends on the nature and specifics of the dataset. Previous studies, such as 
Santos et al. (2020), have identified that conventional machine learning techniques like 
linear regression (Botha and Sheppard 2016) may not be sufficient for creating precise 
models of tight carbonates and other complex pore structures. This is primarily due to 
the highly nonlinear correlations between the input variables and the predicted out-
put. In the quest to understand the physics of transport in porous media, it is crucial to 
employ a model with extensive applicability. This model should be capable of general-
izing across different domains (including those not used in training) and understanding 
complex relationships, such as the link between geometrical structure and permeability 
(Santos et al. 2021).
Given these requirements, we opted for neural networks in our modeling process. 
Neural networks are known for their exceptional ability to learn from vast amounts 
of data, making them suitable for our purposes. Alongside neural networks, we also 
explored Support Vector Regression (SVR), another powerful machine learning algo-
rithm, to compare its performance and effectiveness in our study.

2.4.1  FeedForward Neural Network
Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are powerful function approximators, mapping inputs to 
outputs through a network of interconnected neurons, each acting as a computational ele-

neurons in the hidden layer, which are subsequently linked to the neurons in the output layer. 
These neuron-to-neuron connections are defined by weights, which are adjusted during the 
training process through backpropagation.

2.4.2  Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameter Tuning
Neural networks have several hyperparameters that can be optimized to enhance prediction 
capabilities (Rezaee and Ekundayo 2022). For this purpose, we explored Bayesian optimi-
zation, an advanced method, and compared its efficacy against traditional grid and random 
search methods. Bayesian optimization is a sequential, model-based technique that selects 
the next set of hyperparameters based on an acquisition function, balancing exploration 
and exploitation. It utilizes a probabilistic model to predict the performance of different 
hyperparameter configurations and is more efficient than grid or random searches. This 
efficiency is due to its ability to guide the hyperparameter search process using a proba-
bilistic model (Zhang et al. 2023; Turner et al. 2021). We employed the Bayesian optimi-
zation functionality of the Keras Tuner, incorporating early stopping to halt less promis-
ing evaluations early, thus improving the efficiency of the search process. The entire setup 
encompasses the subsequent configurations:
	
I.	
Search space: We allowed the optimizer to explore (1) the number of neurons per 
hidden layer (ranging from 16 to 512), (2) potential variations in learning rate (1e-5 
to 1e-3) and (3) L2 regularization coefficients.
	 II.	
Objective function: The tuning targeted MSE on a validation subset. After each 
training run, the optimizer updated its probabilistic model to propose the next hyper-
parameter set, balancing exploration and exploitation.
	 III.	
Iterations and early stopping: We typically performed ~ 10–40 Bayesian iterations, 
with a patience mechanism to halt training if validation MSE plateaued for a set 
number of epochs. This minimized overfitting and computational costs.
	 IV.	
Resulting optimal settings: Table 2 for the MLP-ANN model (and Table 3 for the SVR 
model) reveals that the best combination included 192–416–80 neurons, a 0.0001 
learning rate, and an Adam optimizer. We also show the final Test MSE = 0.5267, 
Test MAE = 0.4292, and ~ 5 h’ total search time for the most successful run.
By integrating Bayesian optimization, we systematically searched the space of possi-
ble layer sizes and hyperparameters, ensuring our final architecture was robust rather than 
derived from ad hoc trial-and-error. While Bayesian optimization is more computationally 
demanding than random search, it is advantageous when dealing with large hyperparameter 
spaces and when each evaluation is time-intensive (Masum et al. 2021).

2.4.3  Transfer Learning
To estimate permeability in low-resolution (LR) images with a larger field of view (FOV), 
which are not suitable for direct simulation, this study employs a Multiscale Artificial 
Neural Network (MSANN) model for sequential regression. This approach identifies rela-
tionships between pore structure characteristics and transport properties, primarily per-
meability, derived from Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) simulations. The challenge of 
generalizing to new samples with distributions and resolutions different from the training 
set is addressed through transfer learning. This technique not only accelerates model con-
vergence but also improves the accuracy of permeability predictions compared to training a 
model from scratch (Haq et al. 2023).
As mentioned before, our proposed MSANN is fundamentally a feedforward neural net-
work designed for regression tasks. It consists of: (1) An input layer to receive 3D Euclid-
ean Distance Transform (EDT) feature vectors. (2) Several hidden layers (three in our case) 
employing ReLU activation. (3). An output layer provides permeability estimates. By keep-
ing the network design, the same, all layers are transferable across resolutions rather than 
requiring scale-dependent modifications. This network preserves a consistent architecture 
when moving from high-resolution (HR) to middle-resolution (MR) to low-resolution (LR) 
images. This consistency simplifies parameter transfer, since the network structure—num-
ber of layers, neurons per layer, and activation functions—remains identical at each resolu-
tion. In addition, it incorporates the same Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT) features 
but drawn from different voxel sizes. Thus, each resolution’s EDT maps feed into the same 
input layer dimensions, albeit reflecting different pore-scale morphologies.

2.4.3.1  Sequential Training Process  We structure the training in a hierarchical fashion 
to replicate a “zoom-out” process from fine-scale details to coarser, larger field-of-view 
structures. We begin by training the MLP on HR EDT features. Each voxel’s distance to 
the nearest solid boundary is converted into a feature, capturing fine-scale pore geometry. 
The training targets known permeability references from LBM simulations carried out on 
HR subvolumes. During this phase, the network learns detailed microporosity features and 
associated flow characteristics. We employ Bayesian optimization to finalize hyperparam-
eters (e.g., number of neurons, learning rate), ensuring the baseline HR model is thoroughly 
optimized.
Once the HR model converges, we copy the entire set of trained weights and biases 
(i.e., parameters of all hidden layers) as initialization for the MR scale. The network is 
then fine-tuned using MR EDT volumes. This preserves the microporosity-specific fea-
ture detectors learned during HR training, while allowing adaptation to the newly vis-
ible coarse-scale heterogeneities at 2 µm. Because the network already has knowledge 
of smaller pore throats, it avoids random initialization and converges more quickly on 
MR data, typically requiring far fewer epochs to reach comparable accuracy. We do not 
freeze any specific layer; rather, we allow the model to adapt to the new scale’s morpho-
logical features while retaining knowledge of smaller-scale pore geometry gleaned from 
HR training.
Finally, we reuse the MR-trained parameters to initialize training on the LR data. 
At this scale, images capture the broadest field of view but the coarsest resolution. 
Although the LR images capture macro-scale heterogeneities, they miss many fine-
throat details crucial for flow. The transferred parameters carry essential morpho-
logical cues gleaned from HR and MR stages. This synergy is particularly valuable 
because LR images, while lacking fine throats, still exhibit large-scale flow pathways 
that are strongly influenced by micro-scale connectivity. We further validate this final 
LR model via K-fold cross-validation to confirm robust performance despite the more 
limited pore detail. This hierarchical approach is informed by standard transfer learn-
ing practice, wherein a model trained on a closely related but more feature-rich dataset 
(HR) transfers to a sparser dataset (MR or LR). The shared morphological patterns,

2.4.3.2  Parameter Transfer Mechanics  The presented transfer learning scheme is real-

predictions are stable and not overfitted.
In this study, we assumed that the overall texture depicted in the images represents 
a single rock and fluid unit, considering the complex pore structure of the carbonate 
sample. We did not investigate clustering or unitization of heterogeneities. The pos-
sibility of including additional imaging levels to cover a broader range of length scales 
is an option for future enhancement. The permeabilities estimated through this method 
for specific rock units can ultimately be integrated into reservoir-scale modeling and 
simulation, enabling effective permeability calculation at the core scale using Darcy 
simulation techniques (Botha and Sheppard 2016).
2.4.4  Support Vector Regression (SVR)
Support Vector Regression (SVR), a variant of the Support Vector Machine (SVM) 
algorithm, is widely used for regression tasks. SVR employs a nonlinear transfor-
mation to map the input data to a high-dimensional feature space, seeking to find a 
continuous function that best approximates the data. The algorithm tackles a convex 
optimization problem by minimizing an ε-insensitive loss function, with the model’s 
complexity and performance influenced by several hyperparameters, such as the regu-
larization factor (C) and the kernel function, along with its parameters. Common ker-
nel functions include the radial basis function (RBF), gamma, sigmoid, linear, and 
nonlinear functions like polynomials (Rezaee and Ekundayo 2022). Previous studies 
have demonstrated SVR as a robust machine learning algorithm for regression chal-
lenges (Rezaee and Ekundayo 2022; Tembely et al. 2021; Liu and Liu 2022).
In this research, we employed SVR to analyze the constructed multiscale dataset, 
aiming for a comparative evaluation with the previously developed ANN model. For 
this purpose, 20% of the high-resolution (HR) and middle-resolution (MR) data was 
reserved for testing, while the remaining 80% was used for training. To assess the per-
formance of the model at the low-resolution (LR) scale, K-Fold cross-validation was 
utilized with K set to 10. The Scikit-learn Python library facilitated data splitting and 
model implementation. Hyperparameter tuning for SVR was conducted using Bayes-
ian optimization and applied through the Scikit-Opt Python library. The results of this

The primary goal of this study was to establish a fast and accurate regression mapping 
between the complex geometry of tight multiscale carbonate porous media and their per-
meability variations using the proposed multiscale ANN model. This approach was neces-

the presence of outliers within these plots indicates potential instances where the model 
struggles with accurate prediction. These could arise due to anomalies in the data or com-

3.2  Transfer Learning vs. Single‑Scale Baseline: A Performance Comparison
In this section we built two separate MLP-ANNs—one exclusively on MR subvolumes, 
and another on LR subvolumes—without utilizing prior HR knowledge. On the other hand, 
we pre-trained an identical MLP on HR data before fine-tuning MR and LR images (The 
transfer learning workflow). This sequential approach allowed the MR or LR network to 
reuse morphological cues derived from the microporous details in HR scans. The learn-
ing curves in Fig. 11 illustrate that transfer learned models begin at a significantly lower 
loss and converge faster with lower final MSE than the baseline, reflecting the inherited 
knowledge from the HR stage. Furthermore, as shown in Table 6 in the test phase, transfer 
learning improves both ­R2 and MSE for MR and LR subvolumes (e.g., ­R2 from 0.8203 
to 0.8442 at MR; from 0.8067 to 0.8360 at LR and reduces MSE). These gains signify 
that incorporation from the HR scale translates into a more accurate and stable final model 
at coarser resolutions. Importantly, the LR network trained from scratch underperforms 
because LR images lose crucial pore-throat details, yet these smaller features still govern 
flow. Meanwhile, transfer learning infuses microporous insights from HR data, enabling 
the model to handle broader fields of view without sacrificing subscale connectivity knowl-
edge. Our workflow is designed to sequentially integrate multiple scales in a single MLP-
ANN, bridging high-resolution microporosity with lower-resolution volumes that cover 
larger, more heterogeneous regions of tight carbonate rocks that direct simulation method 
such as LBM is inaccurate and costly. This step-by-step knowledge transfer has not typi-
cally been applied in the most DRP studies reliant on single-scale neural networks or large 
CNN architectures. By pretraining at HR, subsequent MR and LR training requires fewer 
epochs, as the network does not start from random initialization. This scale-aware advan-
tage conserves computational resources while retaining microporous information crucial 
for flow pathways and confirm that transfer learning is not just an alternative approach but 
a distinct improvement in scale-based knowledge.

essential connectivity information. Such a multiscale knowledge transfer is, to our knowl-

methodology specifically targets images of coarser resolution but larger FOV, ensuring 
that macro-scale heterogeneities are included in the analysis. We then fill in the missing

synergy of scales offers a new angle on balancing resolution and FOV without resorting

3.3.3  Practical Applications
Through a careful combination of Bayesian optimization, k-fold cross-validation, and trans-
fer learning, this MLP-based method provides a feasible option for both research facilities 
and industrial settings. It can be trained on widely available CPU hardware within ~ 6 h, 
making it accessible to environments that do not have supercomputers or specialized GPU 
clusters. The method is particularly well-suited for analyzing low-resolution but large-FOV 
images, which often contain macro-scale heterogeneities that are critical to accurate per-
meability estimation.
3.3.4  Planned Future Extensions
This work is a foundation for more advanced approaches to multiscale modeling. Incorpo-
rating partial CNN layers for high-resolution features or exploring ensemble methods may 
bring the MLP-ANN’s predictive performance closer to that of large 3D CNNs, yet retain 
the significantly reduced computational footprint. We also intend to extend this lightweight 
approach to a broader range of rock types—such as shales and sandstones—to further vali-
date its generalizability and applicability. Overall, although 3D CNNs remain state-of-the-
art for maximum accuracy, our central question in this paper is how close we can get to that 
predictive power with an MLP-ANN that is faster to train and does not require specialized 
hardware. Our results confirm that a well-optimized MLP-ANN featuring transfer learn-
ing and EDT-based feature encoding can achieve practical and robust permeability predic-
tions across multiple resolutions, all while drastically reducing computational time (about 
20-fold) and overall resource demands. This advance makes multiscale digital rock physics 
more feasible in settings where large datasets and high-end GPU resources are unavail-
able. On the other hand, while our primary benchmark is the 3D CNN from prior work, 
we also reference traditional direct numerical simulation (e.g., LBM) that can be extremely 
time-consuming for the HR REV images (simulation time ~ 8 h per each volume) and 
unpractical for large, low-resolution domains. By focusing on a CPU-friendly multiscale 
MLP-ANN pipeline, we produce resolution-aware permeability predictions for these larger 
volumes in mere seconds—unfeasible with direct LBM at comparable voxel sizes.

In this study, we extensively evaluated and interpreted our developed multiscale 
regression model to highlight its accuracy and generalizability. We employed a range 
of metrics and statistical graphics tools for this purpose. Our study utilized a carbonate 
sample characterized by a wide variety of pore morphologies, from fine to coarse, mak-
ing it an ideal subject for exploring the correlations between rock characteristics and 
fluid flow transport properties using advanced machine learning techniques.
However, it is important to recognize that the present study relies on a rock sample 
taken from a relatively narrow zone within a single carbonate formation, which may 
constrain the broader applicability of our findings. Our primary objective, nonetheless, 
was to demonstrate a viable proof of concept for a multiscale, transfer learning-based 
workflow under realistic computational constraints. By integrating EDT feature encod-
ing, Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning, and a CPU-based training pipe-
line, this approach can be adapted to other rock types and exploit labeled data from 
various scales.
In future research, we plan to deepen our understanding of the impact of sub-plug loca-
tion variability and incorporate a wider range of resolutions containing heterogeneous fea-
tures in the training set, including fractures, vugs, and two-phase transport properties. We 
also aim to acquire or integrate publicly available micro-CT datasets and sphere pack-based 
images (e.g., from the Digital Rocks Portal) and extend the workflow to other lithologies, 
such as sandstones or shales with diverse image resolutions. These expansions will allow 
us to rigorously evaluate the pipeline’s performance across different pore geometries and 
mineralogies and thus comprehensively establish its generalizability. Taken as a whole, this 
proof-of-concept workflow underlines the potential to reproduce crucial transport proper-
ties at multiple scales, addressing the persistent challenge of balancing imaging resolution 
with field of view in digital rock physics. The hierarchical gains offered by the ANN model 
are most striking in its estimates of effective permeability, which effectively integrate 
diverse pore body and throat sizes at varying resolutions. By laying this methodological 
foundation, we open avenues for subsequent investigations to test and refine the approach 
on a broader spectrum of geological contexts.

4  Conclusion
This paper introduces a computational workflow designed to estimate transport properties 
from lower-resolution, larger-scale micro-CT images of heterogeneous carbonate sam-
ples. Recognizing the inherent tradeoffs between resolution and field of view in digital rock 
imaging devices, our study explored a data-driven approach to overcome these limitations. 
The primary objective was to assess the feasibility of predicting effective permeability var-
iations using low-resolution X-ray micro-CT images, which cover a more representative 
field of view of heterogeneous systems but lack detailed pore system geometry, crucial for 
direct numerical simulations.
To bridge this gap, we integrated advanced digital rock physics (DRP) techniques with 
machine learning approaches, operating across three scales of micro-CT image resolu-
tions. By integrating these resolutions, we could correlate transport property estimations, 
specifically effective permeability, from high-resolution images to lower-resolution ones 
with a broader field of view (FOV). This was facilitated by image registration techniques 
and voxel-to-voxel integration to identify overlap regions, enabling the observation of the 
same transport property across multiple resolutions. The study employed two advanced 
machine learning models—Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Support Vector Regres-
sion (SVR)—to predict permeability variations across these resolutions. The model archi-
tectures were fine-tuned using Bayesian optimization and enhanced through transfer learn-
ing, allowing for scalable permeability prediction that accommodates different levels of 
pore heterogeneity.
Our comprehensive analysis demonstrated the superior performance of the ANN model 
over the SVR model.  This superiority was quantitatively confirmed  as the ANN model 
achieved higher overall R-squared values of 0.863 and lower MSE of 0.196 for low-reso-
lution testing data, compared to the SVR model’s R-squared of 0.734 and MSE of 0.274. 
The ANN model’s predictions are closely aligned with high-resolution target permeabil-
ity values from Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) simulations, indicative of its ability to 
accurately capture complex pore structures. Visual comparisons through histograms fur-
ther confirmed the ANN model’s proficiency in replicating LBM’s permeability distribu-
tion. While the SVR model remained a viable option, particularly for low-resolution data, 
it generally lagged behind the ANN model in matching LBM reference data. The success 
of transfer learning in the ANN model underscores its potential for generalizing from high-
resolution training data to accurately predict lower-resolution permeability, a significant 
advantage for analyzing large datasets.
This study emphasizes the need for carefully selecting machine learning models tai-
lored to specific tasks in digital rock physics, especially those addressing the resolution 
field-of-view tradeoff. The proposed methodology is adaptable to various types of com-
plex multiscale porous media and sets the stage for future research endeavors. These could 
include exploring ensemble methods that capitalize on the strengths of different models or 
developing advanced deep learning architectures to further enhance prediction accuracy 
and generalizability across multiple image resolution scales. Additionally, we intend to 
investigate more formal methodologies in our forthcoming developments, such as Bayesian 
techniques or Monte Carlo Dropout, which generate uncertainty intervals for predictions.

Abstract: Digital rock physics has increasingly become an emerging field in which advanced numeri- cal simulation and high-resolution imaging are combined to accurately predict rock prop- erties. In this context, multiscale imaging is crucial for fully capturing the inherent het- erogeneity of natural rocks. However, limitations in resolution and field of view (FOV) present significant challenges. Direct numerical simulations at large scales are often not computationally practical or may be too expensive. The compromise between FOV and resolution is particularly pronounced in the complex multiscale pore structures of porous rocks, including carbonates in particular. To address this issue, we propose an innovative machine learning technique that integrates multiscale imaging data at varying resolutions. For the rock sample, we used the imaging data published by Nabipour et al. (Adv Water Resour 104695, 2024) in three resolutions. Our approach employs an optimized neural net- work design combined with a transfer learning strategy, enabling the identification of com- plex cross-scale correlations that were previously unattainable with conventional methods. The results demonstrate that this multiscale neural network approach effectively estimates permeability by analyzing various aspects of pore morphology across different scales. In particular, we achieved high accuracy, as evidenced by R-squared coefficients of 0.966 for training and 0.836 for testing in low-resolution domains, and also significantly enhanced computational efficiency, reducing the overall computational time. Despite being tested for images of carbonate rocks, the developed method is adaptable to a wide range of multiscale porous materials and offers a promising solution to the persistent challenge of balancing imaging resolution with FOV.
